items.question: According to Newton's Third Law, when a swimmer pushes against the water, what happens?
options: The water pushes back on the swimmer with equal force, moving them forward
Nothing happens to the swimmer
The water moves but the swimmer stays still
The swimmer sinks
items.correct_answer: The water pushes back on the swimmer with equal force, moving them forward
items.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When the swimmer pushes water backward, the water pushes the swimmer forward.

items.question: Apply Newton's Third Law to design a solution for moving a heavy box across a frictionless floor without touching it directly. You may only use other objects. Explain the forces involved and how they follow Newton's Third Law.

rubric.4: Creative solution (throw objects opposite direction, use compressed air, etc.) with clear explanation of action-reaction force pairs and how momentum is transferred
rubric.2: Solution present but force explanation incomplete
rubric.1: Idea without Newton's Third Law connection

items.question: Two forces act on a stationary object: 10 N to the right and 10 N to the left. What will happen to the object?
options: It will remain stationary because the forces are balanced
It will move to the right
It will move to the left
It will move in circles
items.correct_answer: It will remain stationary because the forces are balanced
items.explanation: When forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, they cancel out (net force = 0). With no net force, the object's motion doesn't change.

items.question: Plan an investigation to provide evidence that the change in an object's motion depends on the sum of forces acting on it AND the mass of the object. Describe: 1) Your materials, 2) Your procedure with controlled variables, 3) What data you would collect, 4) How you would analyze results.

rubric.4: Complete investigation: use cart/track/force meter, test different forces with same mass then same force with different masses, measure acceleration, analyze that a=F/m relationship emerges
rubric.2: Basic investigation but variables not well controlled

items.question: A student brings a magnet closer to a paper clip. The paper clip starts to move toward the magnet when it is 3 cm away. What factor determines when the paper clip starts to move?
options: The strength of the magnetic field decreases with distance
The paper clip decides when to move
Paper clips only move at exactly 3 cm
The magnet becomes stronger when closer
items.correct_answer: The strength of the magnetic field decreases with distance
items.explanation: Magnetic force decreases with distance. At 3 cm, the magnetic force became strong enough to overcome friction and move the paper clip.

items.question: Design a data collection procedure to determine how the strength of a magnetic force changes with distance. What questions would guide your investigation? What data would you collect? Create a sample data table.

rubric.4: Clear questions (How does distance affect force?), procedure (measure force at multiple distances), data table with distance and force columns, prediction that force decreases with distance squared
rubric.2: Some procedure but data collection unclear

items.question: Construct and present an argument using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects. Use examples from everyday life and the solar system.

rubric.4: Strong argument with multiple evidence types: objects fall toward Earth (attractive), more massive planets have more moons (mass matters), you weigh less on moon (mass matters), tides caused by moon's gravity
rubric.3: Good argument with several pieces of evidence
rubric.2: Basic argument with limited evidence

items.question: Conduct an investigation to demonstrate that magnetic or electric fields exist between objects not in contact. Design your investigation, predict what you will observe, and explain how your observations provide evidence for fields.

rubric.4: Clear investigation (compass near wire with current, or iron filings around magnet), prediction of field effects, explanation that action at a distance indicates field presence, field visualization
rubric.2: Investigation shows effect but field concept weak
rubric.1: Describes magnets working without field explanation

items.question: A 2 kg ball traveling at 3 m/s has kinetic energy of 9 J. A 2 kg ball traveling at 6 m/s has kinetic energy of 36 J. Construct a graphical display of this data and describe the relationship between speed and kinetic energy. What mathematical relationship does this suggest?

rubric.4: Accurate graph showing curved relationship, identifies KE quadruples when speed doubles, states KE proportional to speed squared (KE = ½mv²)
rubric.2: Graph created but relationship not clearly stated

items.question: Develop a model to describe how potential energy is stored in a system when objects interact at a distance. Include: 1) A gravitational example, 2) An electromagnetic example (like charged particles), 3) How the arrangement of objects affects the energy stored.

rubric.4: Both examples with correct energy relationships: gravitational PE increases with height/distance from Earth; electric PE depends on charge arrangement; clear connection between position and energy storage
rubric.2: One example well developed

items.question: Construct an argument to support the claim that when the kinetic energy of an object changes, energy is transferred to or from the object. Use a specific example (like braking a car) and explain where the energy goes.

rubric.4: Clear argument: car braking example, KE decreases, energy transfers to brake pads (heat), tires (friction/heat), sound; conservation of energy maintained, energy transformed not destroyed
rubric.3: Good argument with energy transfer explained
rubric.2: Example given but energy transfer incomplete
rubric.1: States energy changes without transfer explanation

items.question: Two sound waves have the same wavelength, but Wave A has twice the amplitude of Wave B. Which statement is correct?
options: Wave A carries more energy than Wave B
Wave B carries more energy than Wave A
Both waves carry the same energy
Amplitude doesn't affect energy
items.correct_answer: Wave A carries more energy than Wave B
items.explanation: The energy carried by a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude. Greater amplitude means more energy.

items.question: Use mathematical representations to describe how: 1) Wavelength and frequency are related (wave equation), 2) Amplitude relates to energy. Draw wave diagrams to support your explanation. Include the equation v = fλ and explain each variable.

rubric.4: Correct equation with variables defined (v=speed, f=frequency, λ=wavelength), wave diagrams showing wavelength/amplitude, explanation that higher amplitude = more energy, frequency increases as wavelength decreases
rubric.3: Equation and diagrams with some explanation
rubric.2: Some elements correct but incomplete

items.question: Develop a model to describe what happens to light waves when they encounter: 1) A mirror, 2) A glass window, 3) A brick wall. Explain the differences in terms of reflection, absorption, and transmission.

rubric.4: Complete model: mirror (mostly reflects), window (mostly transmits, some reflects), wall (mostly absorbs, some reflects); explains that material properties determine which behavior dominates
rubric.3: All three materials with correct primary behavior
rubric.2: Some correct but not all three complete

items.question: Integrate information to support the claim that digitized signals are more reliable than analog signals for encoding and transmitting information. Compare how each type of signal can be affected by noise, and explain why digital signals can be reconstructed more accurately.

rubric.4: Clear comparison: analog signals degrade with noise (static in radio), digital has discrete values (0,1) that can be regenerated; digital can detect/correct errors; examples from technology (CD vs vinyl, digital vs analog TV)
rubric.2: Some digital advantages but comparison weak
rubric.1: States digital is better without explanation

items.question: Develop a model to describe why mutations in genes may result in harmful, beneficial, or neutral effects on the organism. Include: 1) Where genes are located, 2) What genes code for, 3) How a change in the gene sequence affects the protein, 4) An example of each type of effect.

rubric.4: Complete model: genes on chromosomes, code for proteins, mutations change amino acid sequence; examples - harmful (sickle cell in severe form), beneficial (lactose tolerance), neutral (silent mutations)
rubric.3: Good model with understanding of gene-protein relationship
rubric.2: Some mutation understanding but protein connection weak

items.question: Develop a model comparing asexual and sexual reproduction. Explain why: 1) Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring, 2) Sexual reproduction produces offspring with genetic variation. Include implications for adaptation.

rubric.4: Complete model: asexual = one parent, identical DNA copy, clones; sexual = two parents, mixing of chromosomes, genetic variation; variation allows adaptation to changing environments
rubric.2: Some differences but genetic mechanism unclear
rubric.1: Lists reproduction types without genetic focus

items.question: Construct an explanation for how genetic variation of traits in a population increases some individuals' probability of surviving in a specific environment. Use the example of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

rubric.4: Complete explanation: bacteria population has genetic variation, some randomly have resistance genes, antibiotics kill non-resistant, resistant survive and reproduce, population becomes mostly resistant; connects to natural selection
rubric.2: Describes resistance but mechanism unclear
rubric.1: States bacteria become resistant without explaining how

items.question: Which technology has allowed humans to most directly modify the inheritance of specific traits in organisms?
options: Genetic engineering/gene editing
Selective breeding
Cloning
Vaccination
items.explanation: While selective breeding changes traits over generations, genetic engineering allows direct modification of DNA to add, remove, or change specific genes.

items.question: Use mathematical representations to support an explanation of how natural selection may lead to increases or decreases of specific traits in a population over time. Create a model showing a starting population with trait variation and how the proportion changes over 5 generations due to selection.

rubric.4: Mathematical model with starting population (e.g., 100 individuals, 20% with trait), selection pressure, calculations showing trait frequency changing over 5 generations, graph of change over time
rubric.3: Model with population changes but calculations incomplete
rubric.2: Shows concept but mathematical representation weak
rubric.1: States traits change without mathematical support

items.question: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence from rock strata for how scientists use the geologic time scale to organize Earth's 4.6-billion-year history. Include: 1) How relative age is determined, 2) How absolute age is determined, 3) Major divisions of the time scale.

rubric.4: Complete explanation: relative dating through superposition and fossils, absolute dating through radiometric methods, major eons/eras with examples of life forms and events that define boundaries
rubric.3: Good explanation with dating methods and some divisions
rubric.2: Some dating concepts but time scale organization weak
rubric.1: States time scale exists without methods explanation

items.question: Analyze and interpret the following data to provide evidence for plate tectonics: 1) Fossils of the same species found on continents now separated by oceans, 2) The shapes of continental coastlines, 3) Seafloor spreading evidence. How does this data support past plate motions?

rubric.4: All three types of evidence analyzed: matching fossils indicate continents were connected, coastlines fit like puzzle pieces, seafloor spreading shows plates moving apart; synthesis explains plate tectonics theory
rubric.2: Some evidence analyzed but synthesis weak

items.question: Define the criteria and constraints for designing a water purification system for a community without access to clean water. Consider: scientific principles of purification, impact on people, environmental impacts, available resources, and cost limitations.

rubric.4: Complete definition: criteria (removes specific contaminants, produces X liters/day, safe for drinking), constraints (budget, local materials, maintenance by local people, environmental sustainability), considers cultural and practical factors
rubric.3: Good criteria and constraints with most factors
rubric.2: Some criteria/constraints but not comprehensive

items.question: Three solar panel designs are being evaluated. Design A: 20% efficiency, $500/unit, 25-year lifespan. Design B: 15% efficiency, $300/unit, 20-year lifespan. Design C: 25% efficiency, $800/unit, 30-year lifespan. Develop a systematic process to evaluate which design best meets the criteria of efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and longevity.

rubric.4: Systematic evaluation with weighted criteria or cost-per-year-per-efficiency calculations, trade-off analysis, justified recommendation with reasoning for weights chosen
rubric.3: Good systematic comparison with most factors
rubric.2: Comparison made but not fully systematic

items.question: Three student teams designed rockets. Team A's rocket flew highest but landed far from the target. Team B's landed closest to target but flew lowest. Team C had medium height and accuracy. Analyze this test data to identify the best characteristics that could be combined into an optimal design.

rubric.4: Thorough analysis: identifies A's propulsion/aerodynamic strengths, B's guidance/stabilization strengths, C's balance; proposes combination with specific features from each; predicts improved performance
rubric.2: Some analysis but combination not fully developed

items.question: Develop a model for iteratively testing and modifying a bridge design to achieve optimal strength-to-weight ratio. Include: 1) Initial design and hypothesis, 2) Testing procedure, 3) How you would collect and analyze data, 4) How you would modify based on failure points, 5) At least two iterations of improvement.

rubric.4: Complete iterative process: initial design with rationale, clear test procedure, data table (weight held, failure point, mass of bridge), first modification addressing failure, second test and modification, comparison across iterations showing improvement
rubric.3: Good iterative process with at least two improvements
rubric.2: Some iteration but process not fully documented
